demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'I have no future' is a broad, severe hopelessness appraisal, while 'others can see what happened to me just by looking at me' implies a visible stigma/marked external sign. For a trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, the latter is hard to justify clinically unless there is disfigurement or public exposure, neither of which is represented elsewhere.

issues.item: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: For a male delivery driver whose trauma was accidentally causing serious injury to another person, the appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him by looking at him is hard to reconcile with the trauma type unless there are visible injuries or marked stigma, which are not otherwise represented. The other selected appraisals centre on guilt and responsibility, so this item pulls toward a different formulation theme and is not well aligned with the otherwise coherent guilt-based negative appraisal pattern.

vignette:
Ravi Patel is a 34-year-old married South Asian American man who works as a delivery driver, and when he talks about the day that changed his life he does not begin with the impact itself but with the seconds just before it, replayed with a punishing clarity. He had been on a tight route, moving through a residential neighborhood in the late afternoon, making repeated stops in a branded delivery van. Children were out on the sidewalk and front lawns, and although he remembers noticing them, what has stayed with him most is his conviction that he did not respond as he should have. In his account, he was the adult in control of a large vehicle on a street where families were present, and that fact has taken on enormous moral weight. A child moved suddenly into the path of the van and was seriously injured. Ravi describes the scene afterward in fragments: the sound of brakes, people running toward the street, the child on the ground, adults shouting for help. What fixed itself in him was not only that someone was badly hurt, but that he was there, behind the wheel, and could not undo what had happened.

In the immediate aftermath, Ravi cooperated with emergency responders and with the investigations that followed, but privately he had already reached a harsh conclusion. He had come to believe, with complete certainty, that he had failed in the most basic responsibility a person can have around others: to protect them from harm. When he says, “I should have protected them,” he does not mean this abstractly. He means that he thinks he should have anticipated movement sooner, driven differently, scanned more carefully, stopped earlier, shouted, done something more than what he did. He returns again and again to the idea that the injury happened because of the way he acted. Even when others have tried to remind him that it was an accident, Ravi hears that as beside the point. In his mind, “accident” does not lessen responsibility. He believes that if he had been a better, more careful, more alert person, the child would not have been hurt.

Over the following months, this interpretation settled into the way he moved through daily life. Driving, which had once been routine, became morally charged territory. Each neighborhood route felt like entering the scene again: narrow streets, parked cars, children’s bikes near driveways, a ball on a lawn. Even when nothing happened, he found himself bracing. At work he slowed markedly in residential areas and lingered at intersections, scanning for movement with an intensity that put him behind schedule. He was not simply being cautious; he was trying to prevent a second failure that he felt would prove something terrible about him. When dispatch called to ask why deliveries were delayed, Ravi did not know how to explain that every child near a curb seemed like a test he had already once failed.

At home, his wife could see how fixed he had become on what he did not do. Ravi talked in loops about the event, not to seek comfort but to prosecute himself. He would sit at the kitchen table after work and go over alternate versions of those few seconds, insisting that he should have reacted faster, noticed more, protected better. What tormented him most was the sense of inaction. Though he had called for help and stayed at the scene, he says he will never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. In his own telling there is always one more action he should have taken, one more decision that might have changed the outcome. The fact that he cannot identify a definitive corrective act has not softened this belief; if anything, it has made it more absolute.

These ideas began to shape his relationships as well. When extended family members encouraged him to move on, Ravi withdrew, feeling they did not understand the seriousness of what he had done. With his wife, conversations narrowed. He was ashamed of how fully the event occupied him and ashamed too of needing reassurance he could not accept. He sometimes looked at ordinary domestic scenes—his wife cooking in the kitchen, children playing outside their apartment complex—and felt an immediate drop in his stomach, accompanied by the thought that other people trust the world to be safe around them, and he is someone who proved it is not.

By the time he sought help, the strain was showing in concrete ways. Work had become harder to sustain because routes through neighborhoods with families were especially difficult for him, and his hesitation on the road had drawn attention from supervisors. At home he was more distant, often preoccupied, and his wife had urged him to talk to someone because she could see that he was living in judgment of himself every day. Ravi came to treatment not because he thinks he deserves relief exactly, but because he is exhausted by the constant replay of responsibility. What frightens him most is that this event reveals his true character—that he is the kind of man who failed to protect another person when it mattered. What he hopes, cautiously and with visible ambivalence, is not to be told that it never happened, but to understand whether there is any way to live with what he believes he did.
